text: Viral diseases that has known cure yet... 1. HIV/AIDS Can be controlled with antiretroviral therapy (ART), but there’s no permanent cure yet. 2. Herpes simplex virus (HSV) Managed with antiviral drugs but not curable. 3. Hepatitis B – Treatments can suppress the virus, but complete cure is rare. 4. Ebola (chronic effects) Survivors can have lingering health issues; no total cure for the virus once infected. 5. Human papillomavirus (HPV) Some strains cause warts or cancer; vaccines prevent infection, but no cure once infected. 6. Alzheimer’s disease Treatments can slow progression but not stop or reverse it. 7.Parkinson’s disease Medications help control symptoms, but there’s no cure. 8. Multiple sclerosis (MS) Can be managed, but not completely cure 9. Sickle cell disease Bone marrow transplant may help in rare cases, but not a general cure. 10 Type 1 diabetes Managed with insulin; no cure yet. 11.Lupus Controlled with medication; no permanent cure. 12. Cystic fibrosis Treatments greatly improve lifespan, but not a full cure 13. Cancer (varies by type) Some cancers can go into remission, but others remain incurable. 14. Chronic kidney disease Can be managed or treated with dialysis/transplant, but no cure for permanent kidney damage. 15. Rheumatoid arthritis Managed with therapy; not cured. #highlightseveryonefollowers2025

text: Whoa-zempic! ​ The next wave of obesity drugs is pushing the limits of weight loss. Roxanne Khamsi November 19, 2025 Medical weight loss might be on the verge of a further revolution. For starters, people will likely have the option of taking a new class of medications that seem to have fewer bothersome side effects, such as nausea—which affects about half the people on Ozempic and similar drugs. Those now-familiar medications target a pathway involving the appetite-regulating hormone GLP-1; the new ones target cell receptors for a different hormone, amylin. AstraZeneca, Eli Lilly, Zealand Pharma, and, of course, Novo Nordisk, which makes Ozempic, are all testing amylin-based obesity drugs. And if the increasing number of new weight-loss medications seems hard to choose from, you might not have to pick just one. Some medications in development, such as CagriSema, go one step beyond, combining components that target amylin and GLP-1 to make even more powerful drugs. In a recent trial, individuals with obesity who took an amylin-based drug called cagrilintide lost about 12 percent of their weight over the course of 16 months. Those on semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic, lost about 15 percent. Those taking CagriSema lost, on average, more than 20 percent. (By comparison, bariatric surgery, a dramatic procedure that reconfigures the digestive system, can cause a person to lose about 30 percent of their weight—but it comes with the possibility of serious complications such as hernias and life-threatening infections.) These new combination drugs are pressing weight loss far enough past the limits of existing drugs that the field of obesity research is facing an unprecedented question: How far should medical weight loss go? Thomas Lutz, who is known by his contemporaries as the “amylin guy,” has been conducting amylin research at the University of Zurich since the early 1990s, beginning only a few years after amylin had been isolated and characterized in pancreatic cells. Some scientists looked at the molecule with suspicion because it had been isolated in deposits within the pancreas of diabetic patients. Lutz and others helped show that it could reduce appetite in animals. But, perhaps partly because of the lingering mystery of why amylin deposits occur in the body, he found that the wider field took quite a while to get interested in his and other amylin researchers’ work. “We were probably considered outsiders by many others in the field,” Lutz told me. Most of his peers were focused on GLP-1, or leptin, or other peptides—molecules made of the same building blocks as proteins, but smaller. “Not many labs really focused on amylin.” The compound has been used as a drug in the past, Lutz said, albeit in less potent incarnations. Pramlintide, an analogue of amylin, was approved by the FDA for treating diabetes in 2005. The formulation degrades rapidly enough that it has to be injected before every major meal, though; cagrilintide sticks around longer and is injected only once a week. Pramlintide also doesn’t have as big an effect on weight loss compared with the more recent array of amylin drugs. In one trial, twice as many people receiving it lost at least 5 percent of their body weight after four months, relative to those receiving the placebo. But that’s a modest effect. Amylin is just one of a bevy of hormones involved in metabolism that pharmaceutical companies are thinking of using as components in future weight-loss therapies. “Companies are kind of going down the list,” looking at peptides that are secreted after meals and might have commercial potential, Kevin Hall, a metabolism scientist and co-author of the new book Food Intelligence, told me. There are drugs in the works that join the action of GLP-1 with that of GIP, a hormone released from the upper intestine, despite uncertainty about how GIP influences appetite. Some companies are looking at drugs based on the hormone glucagon. Others are investigating peptide YY, a gut hormone that signals to the brain that a meal has been consumed. Because the body tends to adapt to drugs that depend on just one hormonal mechanism, combination medications that target multiple hormones should yield more effective treatments, Beverly Tchang, an endocrinologist at Weill Cornell Medicine who’s on the governing board of the Obesity Society, told me. As the available combinations increase and the weight-loss effects presumably nudge up as well, the question becomes: How much weight loss should these medications aim to produce? “The fact that we have to ask that question is crazy,” Tchang said. “Five years ago, we couldn’t ask that question, because we weren’t hitting these thresholds.” For many individuals with obesity who lose about 5 percent of their weight, their blood levels of certain fat molecules start to improve. At about 10 percent weight loss, their risk of heart attack and stroke typically goes down. When weight loss reaches more than 15 percent, some people start to see the resolution of health problems that often go hand in hand with obesity. “It’s not that their high blood pressure is only getting better,” Tchang said. “It’s going away.” But not everyone sees their risk factors go away when they lose 15 or 20 percent of their weight, which is one reason doctors see a market for more potent drugs. Many people who are morbidly obese need to shed a higher percentage of weight to achieve certain health goals, which is why some undergo bariatric surgery, even with all of its associated risks. Of course, people who are less obese might not benefit from losing a lot of weight. “Not all of our patients need 20 percent, 25 percent, 30 percent weight loss,” Timothy Garvey, an endocrinologist and professor at the University of Alabama at Birmingham who has led trials of amylin drugs, told me. “In fact, it’s unhealthy for many people, and it’s way beyond what we need to improve health.” Doctors often consider body mass index (the imperfect but broadly used measure based on someone’s weight and height) to judge if someone is over- or underweight: A BMI of less than 18.5 is considered underweight. If someone’s weight loss causes their BMI to fall below that in a clinical trial, the person generally has to leave the experiment. But social pressures to lose weight can be tremendous, and GLP-1 drugs are already available at online pharmacies, where physician oversight is less rigorous. Some doctors worry that if more potent combination drugs come along—at the same time that generic GLP-1 drugs are available—people might take their weight loss too far. Since GLP-1 drugs have been widely available, people have used them not just to tend to their health but also to modify their appearance. Christoffer Clemmensen, an obesity researcher at the University of Copenhagen, drew a parallel between the excessive use of weight-loss medications and inappropriate uses of anabolic steroids to bulk up muscles. Without support from a doctor or other medical professionals, people using these drugs, or even more effective ones, could lose significant muscle mass, Michael Lyon, the medical director of the Obesity Medicine and Diabetes Institute in a suburb of Vancouver, British Columbia, told me. In some rare cases, people’s weight loss on GLP-1 drugs doesn’t level off. “They just keep losing and keep losing,” Garvey said. “You are losing bone; you’re losing muscle.” Already, people who want to lose weight have some of the most powerful tools ever available. In the next year, they’ll likely have even more options.

text: Has anyone been in persistent AFib for 6-9 months and had their SR successfully restored to normal? Mine was discovered during a routine dr visit in Sept. I was diagnosed with SVT and underwent an unsuccessful ablation in early 2020. I never had any symptoms and if not for my Apple Watch sending me alerts as my heart rate climbed to 200+,I would not have known. At the time of the ER visit for SVT the medical team stopped and restarted my heart with Adenisine. I was put on Metoprolol Tartrate which I stayed on for 5 years. I had sporadic short episodes of rapid heart rate that would go back to normal so did not think much about it when I started getting AFib alerts earlier this year on my watch. I also have a Kardia Mobile device and looking back at the history it appears I have been in persistent AFib since Jan or Feb. I had no symptoms. Fast forward to Sept 2025. I saw a new cardiologist as I now reside in a different state. She put me on Nebivilol and Eliquis and stopped Metoprolol. I’ve had a Nuclear Stress Test, a Carotid Artery Scan, an Echocardiogram, and a Sleep Study. All showed no issues. I had an unsuccessful Cardioversion last Thursday (SR was not able to be restored) and was put on Flecainide afterwards. As of this morning I am still in AFib and seeing cardiologist at noon today. My resting heart rate is around 62 and my blood pressure is good. BPM range from 50 to 85 most days. I’m guessing she will increase the dosage of Flecainide. FYI, I am 69 years old. Being overweight seems to be the only trigger I have as I do not smoke or drink alcohol or caffeine. I have made an appt with an EP on 12/23. I’m not exactly happy with my current cardiologist as her office feels like an assembly line. I am feeling out of breath from the drugs and pretty stressed out right now.

text: UNDERSTANDING VACCINES VS COVID VACCINES It is important to understand the difference in the mechanism of action between traditional vaccines and the Covid-19 genetic ‘vaccines’. I have summarised and simplified the paper attached for ease of consumption: The mechanism of ‘traditional’ vaccines consists in inoculating viruses, which have been previously inactivated (e.g. by thermal treatments), or attenuated (e.g. by multiple passages in suboptimal growth conditions). Such viruses, which lost the ability to cause acute infection, allow the immune system to recognize them as exogenous pathogens, promoting the production of specific antibodies and memory-T lymphocytes which will kill the virus. On the contrary, the genetic vaccines against COVID-19 induce human cells to produce the spike protein, producing an autoimmune reaction against all the cells that intake the genetic material and start the protein synthesis. (This is what experts call VAIDS - Vaccine Aquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome.) As concerns the Covid vaccine, it is injected into the deltoid muscle, which drains primarily to the axillary lymph nodes. Theoretically, the lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) in which the mRNA is encapsulated, should have a very restricted biodistribution; injected in the deltoid muscle which primarily drains to the axillary lymph nodes. However, a pharmacokinetic study performed by Pfizer for the Japanese regulatory agency shows that the LNPs display an off-target distribution on rodents, accumulating in organs such as the spleen, liver, pituitary gland, thyroid, ovaries and in other tissues. Similarly, the results of the European Medicines Agency (EMA) assessment reports show an off-target distribution of the LNPs used by Pfizer/BioNTech and Moderna, in the liver and other organs of rodents. In conclusion, it is essential to underline that every human cell that intakes the LNPs and translates and expresses the viral protein is inevitably recognized as a threat by the immune system and killed. There are no exceptions to this mechanism. The severity of the resulting damage and the consequences for health depend on the quantity of the cells involved, on the type of tissue and on the strength of the following autoimmune reaction.

I have summarised and simplified the paper attached for ease of consumption: The mechanism of ‘traditional’ vaccines consists in inoculating viruses, which have been previously inactivated (e.g. by thermal treatments), or attenuated (e.g. by multiple passages in suboptimal growth conditions). Such viruses, which lost the ability to cause acute infection, allow the immune system to recognize them as exogenous pathogens, promoting the production of specific antibodies and memory-T lymphocytes which will kill the virus. On the contrary, the genetic vaccines against COVID-19 induce human cells to produce the spike protein, producing an autoimmune reaction against all the cells that intake the genetic material and start the protein synthesis. (This is what experts call VAIDS - Vaccine Aquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome.) As concerns the Covid vaccine, it is injected into the deltoid muscle, which drains primarily to the axillary lymph nodes. Theoretically, the lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) in which the mRNA is encapsulated, should have a very restricted biodistribution; injected in the deltoid muscle which primarily drains to the axillary lymph nodes. In conclusion, it is essential to underline that every human cell that intakes the LNPs and translates and expresses the viral protein is inevitably recognized as a threat by the immune system and killed. There are no exceptions to this mechanism. text: I've been looking for this group. Diagnosed with Stage 2B Lung Cancer NSCLC, Lower Right lobe (RLL) lobectomy in 2023. Never smoked. EGFR atypical mutations: EGFR Exons 18 and 21. The FDA didn't approve Tagrisso for atypical EGFR, so Kaiser wouldn't prescribe it. I found a clinical trial an hour from me for atypical EGFR & Tagrisso. Taking Tagrisso for over 2 years, in a 5-year study. Every 3 months, lab tests, EKG, ECHO, and see study oncologist. Every 6 months, a CT scan and an eye exam. AstraZeneca covers the study. Kaiser treats all side effects. Taking 40 daily because at full dose could not function. Even with the lower dose, I lost my hair, wear wigs. See a podiatrist for toenail edges trimmed down to the nailbed. See a dermatologist for rashes. PT for lymphedema. Digestive issues. Even with the side effects, I am grateful. I'm 77 and write, host my podcast, share stories, speak, and enjoy every day I'm alive.

text: I got my 1st afib attack in 2023 after watching my sister pass away. Went to cardiologist next day and told it was afib. He gave me eliquis put me on a monitor and told me not to worry. Sent me to an EP. I was scared and confused. EP suggested unexplainable procedures which was confusing me more so he told me to come in 2 mo. and he would put another monitor on me . I changed Drs to a highly recommended cardiologist and EP. During my wait for appt. I felt fine . Was put on flecanide besides my metropolol and eliquis and all hell broke loose. Was having afib ,sob, low heart rate and much anxiety. Was told i had bradycardia and needed a pacemaker. 3 days after implant was back in the CCU unit for 5 days with a tube in my side for pericardial infusion. Now I have to push myself to do the things I've always done because my body aches all over and am always tired. I know my story is long but am sick of people who never had afib telling me afib is nothing and it won't kill you.Wishing you all good health.

text: Lebanon’s Ministry of Health has announced that the HPV vaccine will soon be offered for free as part of the national immunization program, a major step in preventing cervical cancer. The vaccine, which normally costs $300–$350, will first be given to adolescent girls, with plans to expand coverage afterward. Health officials say the move is essential to reduce cervical cancer risk in Lebanon, where early screening and vaccination together offer the strongest protection. Distribution is expected to begin in the first phase of 2026, alongside nationwide awareness campaigns encouraging regular screening for women.

Sometimes there’s wheezing too.

He replied "you must be one of those Trump people."

I replied, "If you mean someone who thinks for himself, yes I am."

He had no solution, so he referred me to a FEMALE eye doctor.

She did a thorough examination, told me everything seemed fine, and said there was nothing she could do.

Next, I went to an allergist and he told me he’d heard other people say that.

Hallelujah - but still no cure.

And so I sit here today, crying like a maniac because I was STUPID ENOUGH to get the vaccine Joe Biden told me to take.

Anyone else ever heard of this mystery disease?

text: BREAKTHROUGH: Study shows COVID vaccines decreased heart attacks and strokes. A major study analyzing health records from nearly 46 million adults has found that the risk of heart attacks and strokes decreased following COVID-19 vaccinations-directly challenging widespread misinformation. Published in Nature Communications, the research tracked individuals from December 2020 to January 2022 and found a 10% reduction in arterial thromboses (such as heart attacks and strokes) after the first vaccine dose. The protective effects were even stronger after second doses and boosters, with a 20% drop for Pfizer/BioNTech recipients and a 27% reduction among those who received AstraZeneca. While the study acknowledged rare risks, including myocarditis and clotting issues-mainly in the weeks immediately after vaccination-these events were extremely uncommon. In contrast, contracting COVID-19 significantly increased the risk of serious cardiovascular complications. Co-author Dr. Samantha Ip emphasized that the findings offer robust support for the safet and long-term health benefits of COVID-19 vaccines. As misinformation continues to circulate online, this study adds to a growing body of evidence showing that the vaccines don't just protect against infection-they may also reduce the risk of some of the deadliest health emergencies.

text: The space between It’s what you do for a friend. I was honored to be asked. One of the last times Jeff Prager called me after several frantic up-and-down days of at-home hospice, his blood oxygen levels are so low they cannot stabilize him. He has me on one phone, and 911 on the other phone as he unlocks his front door, Prager groans and collapses — dropping the phone that has me on the other end as they load him onto the gurney…so I know he’ll be taken care of.. I dial it again. An eternally cheerful recorded voice announces the message box is full. Once in the hospital’s hospice, he is put on stronger oxygen, morphine. Calls me every hour, as he feels stronger, then weaker, then frightened, then better., even hopeful!…for the next 24 hours. He asks me to make some phone calls for him with instructions, and I do. Our dance of endings, and only he can hear the beat of it. Midnight on a Sunday, I text I’ll be up for a while longer, just shutting my eyes for a bit — but repeating that I’m right here, to let me know what he needs, to call no matter the time. At 4:38 a.m., the flip-phone I have up under my heart, rings. “Stay with me, don’t leave.” Of course. Then, a raspy: “Talk. About anything. Just talk.” I go over his abstract highlights on several of his key published articles from academia.edu. About how his books and essays have restructured truth-telling in the academic medical field in the last five years. Read to him from “The Pfizer Papers” we had previously both bought and devoured. Chapter and verse, man. Then, oh, my God: A thin voice. “Hold my hand.” From a thousand miles away. Absolutely. He is closer, closing in. I remind him that, as an investigative journalist, he must find a way back to me with a complete report from the other side of what went down, his observations. “Find Einstein. Hell — find Christopher Hitchens! There’s an interview!” This last part of his journey reminds how time as we imagine we know it means nothing, really. Like a tide that slides away, and you wait for it to come back and it does not. As his last horizon eases into view in this dimension, the hour is passing and his wife, Ann, who has end-stage Parkinson’s, will be moved into Prager’s room. It is this interim time — this space in between where a song on vinyl ends and a new one begins, that he fears being alone. That he will slip off, with no one there to hold his hand. His wife comes in finally, and I say, Jeff, here’s Ann, I’ll let you guys go. I hear her stronger voice and his weaker one: “No! Stay with us. Stay.” Of course. Her soft voice to him, his barely audible replies. A little after 7 a.m., the steady beep-beep stops, then stretches suddenly into the steady tone, the last long goodbye. I say mine and gently hang up. -J

text: European stock markets pushed higher Wednesday, helped by progress towards further U.S. stimulus, while Italian political developments and corporate earnings will also share the spotlight. At 3:50 AM ET (0850 GMT), the DAX in Germany traded 0.6% higher, the CAC 40 in France rose 0.4%, U.K.'s FTSE index climbed 0.3%, while Italy’s FTSE MIB rose 2.2%. Former European Central Bank head Mario Draghi is set to meet the Italian President Sergio Mattarella later Wednesday with a view to heading up a government of national unity, something that would end the latest political crisis in Rome. This comes after party leaders failed to agree on a new coalition following the resignation of Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte last week. In corporate news, Siemens (DE:SIEGn) stock rose 2.1% after the German manufacturing conglomerate lifted its full-year guidance, citing faster-than-expected recoveries in China and Germany following the Covid-19 downturn. Banco Santander (MC:SAN) stock rose 2.6% after the Spanish bank declared a cash dividend for 2020 at the maximum level allowed in accordance with the limits set by the European Central Bank, despite recording its first ever annual loss ever. Novo Nordisk A/S (NYSE:NVO) stock added 3.9% after the diabetes drug maker gave upbeat sales and profit forecasts for 2021, while Swedish truckmaker Volvo (ST:VOLVb) stock rose 0.3% after raising its forecasts for some of its main markets and rolling out a hefty shareholder payout. On Tuesday, the U.S. Senate began debating a budget resolution for 2021, the first step towards passing a $1.9 trillion stimulus package proposed by President Joe Biden without Republican support. Additionally, the roll-out of vaccines in many countries is slowly gathering pace: the U.K. has now inoculated 10 million of its population, although health authorities remain concerned by the spread of new variants of the Covid-19 virus. AstraZeneca (LON:AZN) has agreed to deliver nine million more doses of its vaccine to the European Union in the first quarter of this year, a region which has been slow on the inoculation uptake. Oil prices edged higher, still around the highest levels in a year after an unexpected fall in U.S. crude oil supply. The American Petroleum Institute reported late Tuesday crude inventories fell by 4.3 million barrels last week, compared with expectations for a small build. Data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration is due later in the day. U.S. crude futures traded 0.6% higher at $55.08 a barrel, after hitting a one-year high of $55.26 on Tuesday. The international benchmark Brent contract rose 0.1% to $57.88, after earlier climbing to $58.05, its highest in more than 11 months. Elsewhere, gold futures rose 0.3% to $1,838.30/oz, while EUR/USD traded 0.1% lower at 1.2035.

text: So I had 3 Covid jabs, all of them being Oxford-AstraZeneca Covid-19 vaccine. On Monday 10th of November I had a massive blood clot go to my brain, causing me to have a stroke. After having a MRI the tests have show that I have actually had two strokes. One that happened previously, and they can’t actually tell when it happened. In January I complained to my doctor that I was getting headaches and my left eye was hurting. He suggested I go and get my eyes tested. So I went got my eyes tested, and the optician saw something in my left eye, and referred me to the eye hospital at QA. The eye hospital said they wanted me to have a MRI which I had in January. After this I would ask my doctor numerous times what was the results of my MRI. His reply was if we don’t hear from them, then that’s usually a good sign. Well it turns out that scan in January actually showed that I had had a stroke caused by a blood clot to my left optical region of my brain. Unfortunately for me, I was not informed that this was the case. And never heard anything until I questioned my doctor today. He was extremely apologetic and could not understand why this has not been brought to his attention so that we could treat the problem back then . As of a result of this negligence I suffered my second stroke which could have been prevented. I am not after sympathy from anyone, but I would like to hear if there is anyone else that had issues with this jab. I was forced to take the jabs as I was working at Petersfield Town Council which was a Covid vaccination Centre and if I refused, I would not have a job. ￼I am not blaming the council as obviously we was all in the dark at the time. The government have used us as guinea pigs, and that’s a result of it. I have lost my life as I knew it . I want answers and I would like to start up a group to speak to people who have experience￼d similar problems as I have had, and try and make sure this does not happen to anyone else. ￼ ￼ Surly the government should be testing all those that have had these jabs for side effects? text: The split "A stra ze neca" stems from memes claiming it translates to "a road to death" in Latin via Google Translate, but fact-checks debunk this as a mistranslation artifact. AstraZeneca's name originates from a 1999 merger: "Astra" from Greek "astron" (star), and "Zeneca" from a corporate demerger, carrying no ominous Latin meaning. In esoteric terms, stars symbolize illumination, not peril.

text: 💕My Ongoing Battle — From Cancer to Adrenal Insufficiency Some of you know of my battle with cancer, but what many don’t realize is that the fight doesn’t always end when the cancer is under control. I want to share something personal and hopefully help bring awareness to others who might be struggling without answers. During my many different chemo treatments, I also had Keytruda treatments, an immunotherapy drug that helps the immune system attack cancer cells. It saves lives — including mine — but at the same time it almost cost me my life. In my case, Keytruda ramped my immune system up so much that it attacked my organs, causing something called adrenal insufficiency (AI) — a condition where my adrenal glands no longer make enough cortisol, the hormone that helps control stress, blood pressure, and energy levels, body temperatures, electrolytes, and more. Now, every single day, I rely on steroid replacement medication just to stay alive. My body can’t produce its own cortisol, which means even a small illness, high stress, dehydration, or missed dose could become dangerous. It’s not something you can “just push through.” Adrenal insufficiency is rare among people who’ve had immunotherapy (i think they said less than 1% chance of this happening) — but it’s underdiagnosed and often misunderstood. Here’s what I wish more people knew: 💡 Adrenal insufficiency is life-threatening if untreated. 💡 It’s not fatigue or laziness— it’s a complete lack of cortisol. My body is crashing. 💡 People living with AI must carry emergency medication at all times. 💡 Stress, illness, or injury can trigger an adrenal crisis — a medical emergency. I’m sharing this not for sympathy, but for awareness. If you know someone who’s been on immunotherapy and is constantly exhausted, dizzy, or fainting — encourage them to ask their doctor to check their cortisol levels. It could save their life. I’m still standing, still fighting, and still grateful for every day. 💪 If my story helps even one person get diagnosed or treated sooner, then it’s worth sharing. #AdrenalInsufficiencyAwareness #CancerJourney #Keytruda #AutoimmuneSideEffects #KeepFighting

The drug can be administered in hospitals during emergencies – and potentially at home in the future. text: GARDASIL SIDE EFFECTS OR CERVICAL CANCER? The clinical trials for gardasil show a rate of serious adverse events being 1.5-2.4% upon reanalysis of the Merck trials done by Tomljenovic/Shaw (2017). This is a typical rate of serious adverse events when compared to all other vaccines, and was also comparable to the control group they used. There were 5 trials that included the Amorphus Aluminum Hydroxyphosphate Sulfate, one that was uncontrolled, and one with a saline placebo, but they pooled the SAEs from all the trials into one control percentage, blurring out the actual rate of SAE’s in the saline placebo group (which only had about 290 participants compared to 18000 total). Comparing this with a low rate of cervical cancer death being 0.008%, why is there such a push for the HPV vaccine with its higher risk than reward ratio? This vaccine has data to prevent precancerous lesions, but we know most of those lesions don’t go on to develop into cancer, and most certainly wouldn’t if there was screening and early treatment. In fact, one study states cervical cancer screening has been the most effective way of preventing cervical cancer. (Hartman 2023) Sources include the WHO/IARC cervical cancer mortality, Tomljenovic/Shaw (2017), SEER USA Cancer Mortality, and Japan FUTURE studies. text: Have a question. Has anyone that is taking daily blood thinners ever gotten another Pulmonary Embolism in the lungs while on the blood thinners? This is why I'm asking. My husband had Bilateral Pulmonary Embolisms in Feb. of this year. He has taken blood thinners (Eliquis) every day since then. At different dr. appointments during the year he has asked if it is possible to get more clots while on blood thinners and each dr. has said No, it is not possible. A month a go he had major back surgery and about a week a go, his left calf has been aching. (he was off his Eliquis a few days before and after his surgery per the doctors orders) When he lays on his back to sleep, the pressure from the mattress makes his calf ache and he says it hurts if he pushes on it. There is no redness, no hard bump in his calf. He says his foot and calf feel a little tight (like it is swollen) I have looked at his leg and to me it does not look swollen, but he said his skin feels tight. AI Overview +6 Understanding CAR-T cell therapy for cancer: Mayo Clinic ... CAR T-cell therapy is a type of immunotherapy that genetically engineers a patient's own T cells to recognize and attack cancer cells. The process involves collecting a patient's T cells, modifying them in a lab to express a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR), growing them, and then infusing them back into the patient to target and kill cancer cells. This treatment has been effective against certain blood cancers, like lymphoma and leukemia, even when other treatments have failed. How it works Collection: A patient's T cells are collected from their blood. Modification: The T cells are genetically engineered in a lab to create CAR T cells. These cells are equipped with a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) that helps them identify and bind to a specific protein on the surface of cancer cells. Expansion: The CAR T cells are grown in large numbers in the lab. Infusion: The CAR T cells are infused back into the patient's bloodstream. Attack: The CAR T cells find and destroy the cancer cells. What it treats CAR T-cell therapy is used to treat certain types of cancer, including some forms of leukemia, lymphoma, and multiple myeloma. Important considerations It is a form of cell-based gene therapy. Some patients may experience significant side effects, such as confusion, seizures, or brain swelling, which require close monitoring. It is not effective for all patients, and some may experience a relapse after the treatment. Lack of transparency..

——-

The underlying issue is equally serious: 

residual plasmid DNA contamination has indeed been detected in Gardasil vials by independent scientists, and it raises deep questions about vaccine manufacturing oversight and transparency.

Let’s walk carefully through what’s known, what’s been independently verified, and why the institutional reaction has been evasive.

 The core issue: plasmid DNA contamination in Gardasil

Gardasil is produced using recombinant DNA technology. 

The vaccine antigen—the HPV L1 major capsid protein—is made by inserting the gene that codes for it into a plasmid vector, which is then expressed in yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) or in the quadrivalent/nonavalent versions, in insect cells (baculovirus system).

That plasmid serves as the genetic template for producing the virus-like particle (VLP) protein. After expression and purification, the plasmid DNA is supposed to be completely removed.

However, independent investigations—most famously by Dr. Sin Hang Lee, a molecular pathologist known for DNA sequencing integrity—found that Gardasil vials contained residual HPV L1 gene fragments bound to aluminum adjuvant nanoparticles. 

In other words, pieces of residual plasmid DNA were still present and physically attached to aluminum hydroxyphosphate sulfate particles within the vaccine.

Why that matters

That discovery is not trivial. Aluminum adjuvants are known to form nano-sized aggregates that can:

•Facilitate cellular uptake and slow release (so-called "depot effect"),

•Potentially transport co-bound DNA into cells, where it could access nuclear compartments.

Residual foreign DNA, particularly when bound to a transfection-like adjuvant, introduces possible risks of:

1Genomic integration:
If those DNA fragments enter host cells, they can integrate into the genome under certain cellular conditions such as inflammation or oxidative stress. 

While the probability per cell may be low, the sheer number of doses administered globally magnifies the potential collective impact.

2Autoimmune reactions:

Persistent immune activation against foreign nucleic acids can trigger autoimmune responses, including molecular mimicry and chronic inflammation syndromes.

3Unknown long-term effects in younger populations:

HPV vaccination programs targeted preteens and teens—populations with developing immune and endocrine systems—before long-term safety studies on DNA-aluminum complexes had been conducted.

What independent findings showed

Dr. Lee’s group (operating independently, not industry-funded) used nested PCR and DNA sequencing on vials from several countries. 

They consistently detected HPV L1 gene sequences—not free-floating, but firmly bound to aluminum particles.

These results suggested that regulatory-quality testing either failed to detect the contamination or ignored it.

When Lee published and submitted evidence to the WHO, FDA, and CDC, the response was bureaucratic deflection:

•WHO’s Global Advisory Committee on Vaccine Safety dismissed it as “biologically insignificant.”

•No independent retesting of Gardasil lots was conducted under public oversight.

•Instead, Lee’s credibility was attacked rather than his data refuted.

Then, in retrospective litigation discovery (e.g., cases brought over Gardasil adverse effects such as postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome or chronic fatigue syndromes), it became clear that Merck’s internal toxicology pipeline had not required assays for DNA-aluminum complexes—a major regulatory blind spot.

Institutional problem, not just a technical one

This isn’t just about trace DNA; it’s about transparency and quality control.

•Both the U.S. FDA and European Medicines Agency (EMA) have thresholds for residual DNA in biologics (10 ng/dose for biotechnological products; even stricter for vaccines).

Yet, no publicly available data confirm that Gardasil consistently met these limits across batch lots.

You fucking loser 

Mentioned in the Paper
- **Limited Data on Certain Vaccine Doses**: The number of individuals receiving a booster dose of ChAdOx1 (AstraZeneca) or mRNA-1273 (Moderna) was too small to reliably evaluate myocarditis risk for these specific scenarios. This reduces the precision and applicability of findings for booster doses of these vaccines.
Potential Misclassification of Outcomes
Myocarditis was identified solely through ICD-10 codes from hospital admissions or death certifications. This reliance on administrative coding could lead to over- or underestimation of true incidence due to diagnostic errors, inconsistent coding practices, or missed mild cases not requiring hospitalization. The authors note: "Reliance on hospital admission codes and death certification for defining myocarditis may lead to over- or underestimation due to misclassification."
Small Subgroup Sizes: In the 13-17 years age group, only 56 myocarditis events occurred overall, with just 16 post-vaccination. This low event count precluded separate risk evaluations for this subgroup, limiting insights into adolescent-specific risks.
Exclusion of Recurrent Events: The analysis focused only on the first myocarditis occurrence, so results for third (booster) doses do not account for repeated events in the same individuals, potentially underestimating cumulative risk.
Inability to Compare Mortality Outcomes**: The study restricted analyses to vaccinated individuals, making it impossible to directly compare myocarditis-related death rates between infected (unvaccinated) and vaccinated groups. This may underestimate mortality risks specifically after SARS-CoV-2 infection alone.
Precision Issues with mRNA-1273
Fewer people received mRNA-1273 compared to other vaccines, and recipients were on average younger (mean age ~32 years vs. mid-40s/50s for others). This smaller sample size reduced statistical precision for this vaccine, and the age difference could confound observed higher risks, as younger age is a known risk factor for vaccine-associated myocarditis.
Inferred Flaws and Weaknesses Based on Study Design
While the authors conducted robustness checks (e.g., sensitivity analyses for reporting delays and exclusions), the design introduces other potential issues:
Incomplete Capture of SARS-CoV-2 Infections**: Only 13.9% of the vaccinated population had a positive test recorded, likely due to under-testing. This could bias comparisons between infection- and vaccination-related risks, as many infections may have gone undetected, leading to underestimation of infection-attributable myocarditis.
Unmeasured Confounders
Adjustments were made for age, sex, and calendar time, but factors like comorbidities, genetic predispositions, prior infections, or behavioral differences (e.g., healthcare-seeking patterns) were not accounted for. In a self-controlled design, this is partially mitigated by within-person comparisons, but residual confounding remains possible, especially for time-varying exposures.
Temporal and Generalizability Constraints Data covered December 2020 to December 2021, capturing early pandemic waves and initial vaccine rollouts with specific variants (e.g., Alpha/Delta). Results may not generalize to later periods with Omicron variants, updated vaccines, or different populations outside England (e.g., varying demographics, healthcare systems, or vaccination policies). The study also excludes unvaccinated individuals for direct infection-risk comparisons.
Short Observation Windows and Event Rarity Risk intervals were limited to 1-28 days post-exposure, potentially missing longer-term effects. With only 2,861 total myocarditis cases (0.007% of the population), rare events in subgroups amplify uncertainty in incidence rate ratios (IRRs), even if overall estimates are robust.
Self-Controlled Case Series Biases This design assumes events are independent across periods and that individuals serve as their own controls

text: Blocking a single protein forces cancer cells to self-destruct Date: November 20, 2025 Source: NYU Langone Health / NYU Grossman School of Medicine Summary: Researchers uncovered a powerful weakness in lung cancer by shutting down a protein that helps tumors survive stress. When this protein, FSP1, was blocked, lung tumors in mice shrank dramatically, with many cancer cells essentially triggering their own self-destruct mode. The work points to a fresh strategy for targeting stubborn lung cancers. Share: FULL STORY Protein Block Makes Cancer Self-Destruct Stopping one protein forces lung cancer cells to self-destruct. Credit: Shutterstock Researchers at NYU Langone Health have identified how a specific form of cell death linked to the buildup of highly reactive molecules can slow the growth of lung tumors. This type of cell death, known as ferroptosis, originally evolved as a way for the body to clear out cells that become overly stressed. Cancer cells fall into this category, yet over time they have developed ways to block ferroptosis so they can continue multiplying even under damaging conditions. Blocking FSP1 Dramatically Weakens Lung Tumors A study published online November 5 in Nature showed that an experimental therapy targeting a protein called ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1) significantly reduced tumor growth in mice with lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). Blocking this protein, which helps cancer cells avoid ferroptosis, shrank tumors by as much as 80%. Lung cancer remains the world's leading cause of cancer-related deaths, and LUAD is the most common form among nonsmokers, accounting for about 40% of cases. "This first test of a drug that blocks ferroptosis suppression highlights the importance of the process to cancer cell survivaland paves the way for a new treatment strategy," said senior study author Thales Papagiannakopoulos, PhD[GW1], an associate professor in the Department of Pathology[GW2] at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine. Reactive Molecules and Their Role in Cell Damage Ferroptosis takes place when iron levels rise inside cells, fueling the production of highly reactive molecules made from oxygen, water, and hydrogen peroxide known as reactive oxygen species (ROS). In small amounts, ROS help cells communicate. In excess, they create oxidative stress, which occurs when ROS add oxygen molecules to vital proteins and DNA, damaging or breaking them apart. ROS can also harm fats that form the outer membranes of cells, contributing to cell death and tissue injury. Blocking FSP1 Shows Strong Tumor-Suppressing Effects To investigate how FSP1 affects lung cancer, the research team genetically modified mice so that their lung cancer cells lacked the FSP1 gene. These mice developed smaller tumors due to increased cancer cell death. The researchers also tested icFSP1, a newer drug designed to inhibit FSP1. Mice treated with icFSP1 lived longer and experienced tumor reductions similar to those seen in mice whose cancer cells were engineered to lack FSP1. The study also found that FSP1 may be a more promising treatment target than another ferroptosis-blocking protein, glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), which has been studied in cancer research for a longer period. The findings suggest that FSP1 is more actively involved in preventing ferroptosis in lung cancer cells while playing a smaller role in normal cell function (which could translate to fewer side effects). Increased levels of FSP1 were also associated with poorer survival rates in human LUAD patients, unlike GPX4. Future Directions and Ongoing Research "Our future research will focus on optimizing FSP1 inhibitors and investigating the potential of harnessing ferroptosis as a treatment strategy for other solid tumors, such as pancreatic cancer," said lead study author Katherine Wu, an MD/PhD student working in the Papagiannakopoulos lab. "We aim to translate these findings from the lab into novel clinical therapies for cancer patients." In addition to Wu and Pagagiannakopoulos, contributors from the Department of Pathology at NYU Langone include co-first author Alec Vaughan, Jozef Bossowski, Yuan Hao, Aikaterini Ziogou, Mari Nakamura, Ray Pillai, Mariana Mancini, Sahith Rajalingam, and Suckwoo Chung. Other study authors include Seon Min Kim, Tae Ha Kim, and Yun Pyo Kang of the College of Pharmacy and Research Institute of Pharmaceutical Sciences at Seoul National University; Mingqi Han and David Shackelford from the Department of Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine at the David Geffen School of Medicine, University of California Los Angeles; Toshitaka Nakamura and Marcus Conrad of the Institute of Metabolism and Cell Death, Molecular Targets and Therapeutics Center at Helmholtz Munich in Germany; and Lidong Wang and Diane Simeone of the Moores Cancer Center, University of California, San Diego, La Jolla. The study received funding from National Institutes of Health grants S10RR027926, S10OD032292, R37CA222504, R01CA227649, R01CA283049, R01CA262562, T32GM136542, T32GM136573, and T32GM136542. Additional support was provided by the American Cancer Society Research Scholar Grant (RSG-17-20001-TBE), the Ruth L. Kirschstein Individual Predoctoral National Research Service Award fellowship (F30CA275258), the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG) (CO 291/7-1 Priority Program SPP 2306 [CO 291/9-1, #461385412; CO 291/10-1, #461507177], the European Research Council under the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation program (grant GA 884754), and the Perlmutter Cancer Center Support Grant P30CA016087. Papagiannakopoulos received funding from the Pfizer Medical Education Group, Dracen Pharmaceuticals, Kymera Therapeutics, Bristol Myers Squibb, and Agios available under an aCC-BY-NC-ND 4.0 international license. These relationships are being managed in accordance with NYU Langone Health policies. Story Source: Materials provided by NYU Langone Health / NYU Grossman School of Medicine. Mice treated with icFSP1 lived longer and experienced tumor reductions similar to those seen in mice whose cancer cells were engineered to lack FSP1. The study also found that FSP1 may be a more promising treatment target than another ferroptosis-blocking protein, glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), which has been studied in cancer research for a longer period. The findings suggest that FSP1 is more actively involved in preventing ferroptosis in lung cancer cells while playing a smaller role in normal cell function (which could translate to fewer side effects). Increased levels of FSP1 were also associated with poorer survival rates in human LUAD patients, unlike GPX4. Future Directions and Ongoing Research "Our future research will focus on optimizing FSP1 inhibitors and investigating the potential of harnessing ferroptosis as a treatment strategy for other solid tumors, such as pancreatic cancer," said lead study author Katherine Wu, an MD/PhD student working in the Papagiannakopoulos lab. "We aim to translate these findings from the lab into novel clinical therapies for cancer patients." In addition to Wu and Pagagiannakopoulos, contributors from the Department of Pathology at NYU Langone include co-first author Alec Vaughan, Jozef Bossowski, Yuan Hao, Aikaterini Ziogou, Mari Nakamura, Ray Pillai, Mariana Mancini, Sahith Rajalingam, and Suckwoo Chung. text: TTS/VITT is primarily associated with adenovirus vector vaccines like J&J and AstraZeneca, driven by anti-PF4 antibodies absent in mRNA vaccines such as Pfizer and Moderna. Confirmed US TTS cases number around 60 with 9 deaths from J&J; mRNA reports lack causal confirmation at scale per CDC and EMA data. VAERS captures unverified signals—thrombocytopenia claims exceed 10K but adjudication attributes causality to <0.001% of doses, dwarfed by COVID's 5-40% incidence and 2-5x mortality multiplier in affected patients.
